chapter_title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces for Game Systems

screens.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces for Game Systems
screens.subtitle: Designing flexible behaviors with C++ abstract bases and Unreal's UInterface

narration.text: In this lesson we will explore two complementary tools for organizing game behavior: C++ abstract classes and Unreal Engine UInterface. You will learn what a pure virtual function is and how an abstract class enforces a common behavior across a family of related types. Then we will show how UInterface allows unrelated actors to share capabilities like interactable or damageable without changing their inheritance chain. This matters because games need objects that can be both 'a type of' something and 'able to do' many different actions at the same time. We will walk through real C++ snippets: declaring a UINTERFACE, implementing a BlueprintNativeEvent, writing an OnInteract_Implementation, and safely calling IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract. Along the way you will see common pitfalls — for example, trying to call an interface method directly or forgetting the I prefix — and practical design guidance on when to prefer an abstract base versus an interface. By the end, you will be able to choose the right contract for your systems and call interface functions correctly in gameplay code.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Abstract classes give shared foundations and enforced behavior for related types; UInterface gives flexible contracts for unrelated types, enabling loose coupling and extensibility.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Overview
Abstract Classes & Interfaces
How to design contracts and call them safely in Unreal C++

This lesson shows two patterns: the abstract C++ base with pure virtual functions for strong "is-a" relationships, and Unreal's UInterface for flexible "can-do" behavior across unrelated classes. We'll use examples like a base enemy behavior and an interactable interface used by doors and pickup items, and show the required Execute_ call that ensures correct dispatch through Unreal's reflection system.

In this lesson
Abstract classes & pure virtual functions
Coming up
UInterface, BlueprintNativeEvent, Execute_
Hands-on
Implement IInteractable and TryInteract
Explore key topics
Three short focus areas to guide your work
Abstract class: pure virtual functions to enforce behavior.
UInterface: implementable by any UCLASS, supports Blueprint overrides.
Execute_ & Implements: safe runtime checking and dispatch.
Visual concept
ABaseEnemy
Defines AttackBehavior() as pure virtual — concrete enemies implement it.
IInteractable
Any actor can implement OnInteract. Use Execute_OnInteract to call it.
Quick takeaway
Use abstract classes to share implementation for a related family. Use UInterface for loose coupling when objects should share behavior without shared ancestry.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives will guide your practice. First, you'll understand what abstract classes are in C++, including pure virtual functions and why they make a class uninstantiable. You'll also implement Unreal Engine UInterface definitions so your actors can declare behavioral contracts. Third, you'll design game systems that combine abstract classes and interfaces to produce robust, extensible architectures. Fourth, you'll learn the exact runtime pattern to call interface functions on UObject-derived instances: checking with Implements and dispatching using the Execute_ prefix. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a short example you can try immediately. For instance, after implementing IInteractable, you'll place an ADoor and APickupItem in the level and interact with both through the same player code. Finally, these milestones map to verified competency steps so you can confirm you can both code and run the interactions successfully in the editor.

screens.title: What is an Abstract Class?
screens.subtitle: Pure virtual functions and enforcing a contract

narration.text: An abstract class in C++ is a class that cannot be instantiated because it declares at least one pure virtual function. A pure virtual function is written by assigning equals zero to the function declaration, for example, virtual void AttackBehavior() = 0;. The point of an abstract class is to provide a shared foundation and to enforce that derived concrete classes implement specific behaviors. In game code this means you can write systems that treat different types polymorphically: a pointer to your base type can call the required function and rely on the derived class to provide the concrete implementation. As a concrete example, imagine an ABaseEnemy that declares virtual void AttackBehavior() = 0;. AZombie and ASpider inherit from ABaseEnemy and provide their own AttackBehavior. The game code can maintain a list of ABaseEnemy pointers and call AttackBehavior on each, without knowing the specific type. A common misconception is that abstract classes cannot contain any implemented code; actually they can include helper functions and common data. Use abstract classes when you have a strong is-a relationship and want shared implementation plus enforced methods. A takeaway question: when you need shared code plus required overrides, could an abstract base make your system simpler?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Abstract class: a base that enforces required methods via pure virtual functions while optionally providing shared implementation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What is an Abstract Class?
Definition
Pure virtual functions enforce derived implementations
Key points:
  • Contains at least one pure virtual function declared with = 0.
  • Cannot be instantiated directly; used as a base type.
  • Can still provide shared helpers and member data.
Example
// ABaseEnemy.h
class ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  virtual void AttackBehavior() = 0; // pure virtual: makes class abstract
  void MoveToTarget(); // shared helper implementation
};

// AZombie inherits and implements the attack behavior
class AZombie : public ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  void AttackBehavior() override { /* zombie-specific attack */ }
};
Concrete example and misconception

You can store heterogeneous enemies in an ABaseEnemy* array and call AttackBehavior on each. A common misconception is that abstract classes cannot contain any implementation; in practice you often implement common utilities in the base and leave only the variable behavior pure virtual.

Key Takeaway

Use abstract bases when types share identity and some implementation, but require specific methods implemented by each derived class.

screens.title: ABaseEnemy Example: Polymorphism in Practice
screens.subtitle: How to use a pure virtual to force behavior across enemy types

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple enemy base pattern that enforces an attack method. The base declares a pure virtual AttackBehavior so derived classes must implement it. This guarantees that code holding ABaseEnemy pointers can invoke the attack without conditional checks. In practice you often combine a pure virtual with shared helpers like MoveToTarget or health management. For example, AZombie implements a melee lunge while ASpider might implement a web shot; both are called AttackBehavior from game loop code. A common error is attempting to create an instance of ABaseEnemy; the compiler prevents this because of the pure virtual. Another subtle point: an abstract base still participates in single inheritance rules — only one base class can be inherited. If you need an object to have multiple orthogonal behaviors, an interface is a better fit. As a hands-on example, create both AZombie and ASpider, add them to the level, store pointers to them in a single array of ABaseEnemy*, and call AttackBehavior on each in a manager class to observe their different runtime behavior. A reflective question: how would you factor shared damage handling into the base while keeping attack styles separate?

keyIdea.title: Polymorphic usage
keyIdea.text: ABaseEnemy enforces AttackBehavior and enables polymorphic calls across varied enemy types.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ABaseEnemy Example
Code: base and concrete types
// ABaseEnemy.h
class ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  virtual void AttackBehavior() = 0; // pure virtual
  void MoveToTarget();
};

// AZombie.h
class AZombie : public ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  void AttackBehavior() override { /* melee logic */ }
};
Compile-time enforcement ensures each concrete enemy supplies its own AttackBehavior. This eliminates run-time type switches when executing attacks.
Practical pattern
  • Manager keeps ABaseEnemy* list and calls AttackBehavior() for each enemy each tick or when triggered.
  • Shared data like health or movement stays in the base to avoid duplication.
  • If an enemy must also be 'interactable' or 'damageable' by unrelated systems, implement interfaces alongside the base.
Common mistake

Trying to instantiate ABaseEnemy will fail. Use concrete derived types for placement and testing.

screens.title: What is a UInterface in Unreal?
screens.subtitle: Defining a behavior contract across unrelated classes

narration.text: Unreal Engine's UInterface is a reflection-aware way to define a contract that any UCLASS can implement. The system uses two declarations: the UINTERFACE class, which derives from UInterface and is the UObject representation, and the I-prefixed C++ class where you place the UFUNCTION declarations. For behavioral contracts, use BlueprintNativeEvent when you want to supply an optional default C++ implementation while allowing Blueprints to override it. The key benefit is that a class can implement multiple interfaces, providing flexible 'can-do' relationships. For example, a Door can be both IInteractable and IDamageable without changing its primary inheritance. Interfaces promote loose coupling: code can check Implements<UInteractable>() and then call the Execute_ wrapper to invoke the function without needing to cast to a concrete type. A common misconception is thinking interfaces replace all base classes; they do not. Interfaces describe capabilities, while abstract bases provide shared implementation and identity. Ask yourself: does the behavior describe what an object is, or what it can do? Use UInterface for the latter. What is a UInterface in Unreal? means uinterface defines capabilities that any uclass can adopt, enabling multiple orthogonal behaviors without changing inheritance.. In practical terms, defining a behavior contract across unrelated classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UInterface purpose
keyIdea.text: UInterface defines capabilities that any UCLASS can adopt, enabling multiple orthogonal behaviors without changing inheritance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › UInterface Definition
Structure of a UInterface
A UInterface has two parts: the UObject wrapper declared with UINTERFACE and the I-prefixed C++ interface where UFUNCTIONs are declared. Use Blueprintable to allow Blueprints to implement the interface and BlueprintNativeEvent for optional C++ defaults.
When to use
When different classes need to share behavior but don't share a common base. Example: doors and pickup items both implement IInteractable.
Misconception
An interface doesn't provide shared implementation. If you need common code, combine an abstract base with interfaces as needed.
Concrete scenario

Imagine a Door and a PickupItem both need an OnInteract function. They may be unrelated classes in the inheritance tree. Adding IInteractable lets the player code interact with either type without knowing its concrete class. This is core to loose coupling and extensibility in gameplay systems.

Key Takeaway

Use UInterface when multiple unrelated classes should expose the same behavior and you want Blueprint compatibility.

screens.title: Declaring IInteractable
screens.subtitle: UINTERFACE macro, I-prefixed C++ interface and BlueprintNativeEvent

narration.text: Here we inspect the canonical pattern for declaring an Unreal interface. The header usually includes CoreMinimal and UObject/Interface, and uses the UINTERFACE macro to declare a UInteractable class deriving from UInterface. The actual C++ contract lives in IInteractable where you declare UFUNCTIONs. Use BlueprintNativeEvent on functions you may want a default C++ implementation for while still allowing Blueprint overrides. When you provide a default, implement the function with the _Implementation suffix in the class that implements the interface. A typical declaration looks like this: UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable) class UInteractable : public UInterface { GENERATED_BODY() }; followed by class IInteractable { GENERATED_BODY() public: UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Interaction") void OnInteract(AActor* InstigatorActor); };. Keep the naming consistent: U-prefixed for the UObject wrapper and I-prefixed for the interface. This distinction is important for the reflection system to wire up Blueprint implementations correctly. Try declaring a simple interface file and compile to ensure no macro errors appear. Declaring IInteractable means uinterface + i-prefixed c++ interface + blueprintnativeevent forms the standard unreal interface declaration pattern.. In practical terms, uinterface macro, i-prefixed c++ interface and blueprintnativeevent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Declaration pattern
keyIdea.text: UINTERFACE + I-prefixed C++ interface + BlueprintNativeEvent forms the standard Unreal interface declaration pattern.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Declaring IInteractable
Header example
// Interactable.h
#pragma once
#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "Interactable.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractable : public UInterface
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
};

class MYPROJECT_API IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Interaction")
    void OnInteract(AActor* InstigatorActor);
};
Key notes
  • UINTERFACE declares the UObject wrapper for the reflection system.
  • I-prefixed class holds the UFUNCTION declarations used by implementers.
  • BlueprintNativeEvent allows an optional C++ default with an _Implementation override.
Pro tip

Keep the generated header name consistent and include the generated .h to avoid macro errors during compile.

screens.title: Implementing IInteractable in a UCLASS
screens.subtitle: Adding public IInteractable and the _Implementation method

narration.text: To implement a UInterface in a UCLASS, add public IInteractable to the inheritance list and implement the function with the _Implementation suffix when the declaration used BlueprintNativeEvent. For example, declare AMyDoor : public AActor, public IInteractable and then define void AMyDoor::OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor) in the. cpp. Inside that function you can add log messages, play animations, or trigger gameplay changes. In Blueprints, the same interface can be implemented and will be called through the Execute_ dispatcher at runtime. One practical unity: use UPROPERTY to expose doors' state like bIsLocked and check it in OnInteract_Implementation to change behavior. Don't forget to include the interface header in both. h and. cpp files. A frequent mistake is omitting the override keyword or using the wrong function name; the compiler will help if the signature or suffix is incorrect. After implementing, place the actor in the level and test the OnInteract behavior from your player code to validate the expected control flow. Implementing IInteractable in a UCLASS means add public iinteractable to your uclass and implement oninteract_implementation when using blueprintnativeevent to provide c++ behavior.. In practical terms, adding public iinteractable and the _implementation method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implement correctly
keyIdea.text: Add public IInteractable to your UCLASS and implement OnInteract_Implementation when using BlueprintNativeEvent to provide C++ behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Implementing IInteractable
Header: add interface
// MyDoor.h
#include "Interactable.h"

UCLASS()
class AMyDoor : public AActor, public IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyDoor();
    virtual void OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor) override;
    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) bool bIsLocked;
};
CPP: provide implementation
// MyDoor.cpp
void AMyDoor::OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor)
{
    if (bIsLocked) {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door is locked!"));
    } else {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Door opened by %s"), *InstigatorActor->GetName());
        Destroy();
    }
}

screens.title: BlueprintNativeEvent and _Implementation
screens.subtitle: How defaults and Blueprint overrides interact

narration.text: BlueprintNativeEvent is a UFUNCTION specifier that enables both a C++ default implementation and an optional Blueprint override. When you mark a function BlueprintNativeEvent, the interface declares the function signature, and implementers provide the C++ behavior in a method with the _Implementation suffix. At runtime, calling via the Execute_ wrapper will dispatch to either the Blueprint override if present or the C++ _Implementation otherwise. This duality gives you powerful flexibility: you can ship a sensible default in C++ for broader systems while letting designers tweak or replace behavior in Blueprints. One subtlety is the naming: implement the function exactly as FunctionName_Implementation to match the generated dispatcher. Another misconception: BlueprintImplementableEvent has no C++ default; BlueprintNativeEvent does. Choose BlueprintNativeEvent when you want a default and designer-specific overrides. As a practical check, after implementing the _Implementation in C++, create a Blueprint class that implements the interface and override the event; test that Execute_ calls the Blueprint version instead of your C++ default. BlueprintNativeEvent and _Implementation means provides a c++ default implementation while allowing blueprint overrides; use _implementation in c++ and execute_ at runtime.. In practical terms, how defaults and blueprint overrides interact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: BlueprintNativeEvent
keyIdea.text: Provides a C++ default implementation while allowing Blueprint overrides; use _Implementation in C++ and Execute_ at runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › BlueprintNativeEvent
Concept

BlueprintNativeEvent enables a default C++ implementation and still allows a Blueprint to override the function. Implement the C++ default using FunctionName_Implementation and use Execute_ to call the function so Blueprint overrides are respected.

Contrast
BlueprintImplementableEvent provides no C++ default; BlueprintNativeEvent does. Choose based on whether you need a C++ fallback.
Test scenario
  1. Implement OnInteract_Implementation in C++ with default behavior.
  2. Create a Blueprint that implements the interface and override OnInteract.
  3. From runtime code call IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(Target, Instigator) and observe the Blueprint override running.
Key Takeaway

Use BlueprintNativeEvent when you want a reliable C++ fallback while keeping designer-friendly Blueprint overrides.

screens.title: Calling Interface Functions at Runtime
screens.subtitle: Safe pattern: Implements check then Execute_ dispatch

narration.text: When you want to call an interface function on a UObject or AActor pointer, the safe runtime pattern is to first check whether the object implements the UInterface and then call the function via the generated Execute_ wrapper. Use TargetActor->Implements<UInteractable>() to test capability. If the check passes, call IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(TargetActor, InstigatorActor). This wrapper ensures proper dispatch, either to the C++ _Implementation or to a Blueprint override, respecting Unreal's reflection and RPC mechanisms. A common mistake is attempting to call TargetActor->OnInteract() directly; that bypasses the reflection layer and will not call the Blueprint override. Another variant is casting to the interface and calling directly, which is less robust across Blueprint/C++ boundaries. For example, inside a player TryInteract implementation, do a line trace, get HitActor, if it Implements the interactable interface then Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this). This ensures predictable behavior and avoids crashing when the actor does not implement the interface. Reflective question: how would you log helpful warnings when an expected interface is missing to aid debugging? Calling Interface Functions at Runtime means check implements<uinterface>() and call iinterface::execute_function to ensure blueprint and c++ implementations receive the call.. In practical terms, safe pattern: implements check then execute_ dispatch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runtime dispatch
keyIdea.text: Check Implements<UInterface>() and call IInterface::Execute_Function to ensure Blueprint and C++ implementations receive the call.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Calling Interface Functions
Pattern
Follow this safe sequence:
  1. Check pointer validity.
  2. Use Target->Implements<UYourInterface>() to ensure the actor supports the interface.
  3. Call IYourInterface::Execute_YourFunction(Target, params) to dispatch correctly.
// Example inside player code
if (HitActor && HitActor->Implements<UInteractable>())
{
  IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this);
}
else
{
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Not interactable"));
}
Common pitfalls
  • Don't call the interface method directly on the actor pointer.
  • Remember to include the interface header where you call Execute_.
  • Use clear logging to help designers understand when an object is missing the expected interface.
Key Takeaway

The Implements check plus Execute_ call ensures reliable dispatch across C++ and Blueprint implementations.

screens.title: TryInteract: Line Trace and Execute_OnInteract
screens.subtitle: Player code that finds and calls IInteractable objects

narration.text: We'll walk through a TryInteract implementation that performs a line trace and calls the interact interface on the first valid hit. The function computes a start and end point from the player's location and forward vector, fires a LineTraceSingleByChannel, and examines the FHitResult. If HitResult returns an actor, check HitActor->Implements<UInteractable>() and then invoke IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this). This pattern avoids direct casting to concrete types and makes the interaction polymorphic and designer-friendly. The code also uses clear logging to indicate whether the hit actor was non-interactable or if nothing was hit, which helps during level testing. Implement this, bind it to an input like the E key, and test by walking up to ADoor and APickupItem instances. If a Blueprint override exists for OnInteract, the Execute_ call will route to that override instead of the C++ _Implementation. A debugging tip: if your Execute_ call does not reach expected behavior, ensure the actor has implemented the interface and that the header and generated includes are present in the compilation unit. TryInteract: Line Trace and Execute_OnInteract means use a line trace, implements check, and execute_oninteract to interact polymorphically with actors in the world.. In practical terms, player code that finds and calls iinteractable objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Player interaction flow
keyIdea.text: Use a line trace, Implements check, and Execute_OnInteract to interact polymorphically with actors in the world.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › TryInteract Walkthrough
TryInteract example
// MyPlayerCharacter.cpp - simplified
void AMyPlayerCharacter::TryInteract()
{
  FVector Start = GetActorLocation();
  FVector End = Start + GetActorForwardVector() * 200.0f;

  FHitResult Hit;
  FCollisionQueryParams Params;
  Params.AddIgnoredActor(this);

  if (GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(Hit, Start, End, ECC_Visibility, Params))
  {
    AActor* HitActor = Hit.GetActor();
    if (HitActor && HitActor->Implements<UInteractable>())
    {
      IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this);
    }
    else
    {
      UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Hit non-interactable"));
    }
  }
  else
  {
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Nothing to interact with"));
  }
}
Test checklist
  • Place ADoor and APickupItem in level and set bIsLocked where relevant.
  • Ensure player pawn is AMyPlayerCharacter and bind TryInteract to the input.
  • Observe on-screen debug messages or logs when interacting.
Common mistake

Forgetting Params.AddIgnoredActor(this) can cause self hits; include it to avoid false positives.

screens.title: When to Use Abstract Class vs Interface
screens.subtitle: Design decision guide for game behaviors

narration.text: Deciding between an abstract class and an interface requires thinking about identity, shared implementation, and orthogonal behavior. Use an abstract class when you have a clear is-a hierarchy and want to share implementation details. For example, if all enemy types share movement logic and health handling, place those in an abstract ABaseEnemy and keep attack behavior as pure virtual. Use an interface when you need a can-do relationship: doors, pickups, NPCs, and crates might all be interactable or damageable without being related by inheritance. Interfaces allow multiple capabilities to be combined on one actor without single-inheritance limits. A practical rule of thumb: if concrete types should be substitutable and share state or code, consider an abstract base. If the behavior is an orthogonal capability that many unrelated classes might adopt, use a UInterface. Beware of overusing interfaces — too many fine-grained interfaces can make code harder to navigate. A small exercise: for a destructible crate that can also be picked up by a character, decide whether you would use a base class, an interface, or both, and justify your choice.

keyIdea.title: Design rule of thumb
keyIdea.text: Abstract base for shared identity and implementation; interface for orthogonal capabilities and loose coupling.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Design Decision
Abstract Class (Is-a)
  • Strong identity: types are members of the same family.
  • Share implementation: common functions and data live in the base.
  • Single inheritance limitation applies.
When to choose
Use when core behavior and state should be shared across all derived types.
Interface (Can-do)
  • Describes capabilities, not identity.
  • Multiple interfaces can be implemented by any class.
  • Promotes loose coupling between systems.
When to choose
Use when unrelated classes should expose the same behavior, like interactable or damageable.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create IInteractable, ADoor, APickupItem, and TryInteract
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to implement and test interfaces in your level

narration.text: Follow this guided activity to cement the patterns. Step one: create a new C++ Interface class by choosing UInterface in the editor and name it Interactable. Replace the generated content with the declared UINTERFACE and the IInteractable contract containing a BlueprintNativeEvent OnInteract(AActor*). Step two: create ADoor and APickupItem AActor classes; add public IInteractable to both headers. Implement OnInteract_Implementation in each. cpp: for the door, check bIsLocked and either log a locked message or open/destroy; for the pickup, log item collected and call Destroy. Step three: create AMyPlayerCharacter and add TryInteract that does a line trace forward, checks Implements<UInteractable>(), and calls IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this). Bind TryInteract to an input and set AMyPlayerCharacter as the default pawn. Step four: place ADoor and APickupItem in the level and test interactions. If you see the correct log messages and Blueprint overrides run if present, you've implemented the pattern correctly. Finally, reflect on how this keeps code decoupled and extensible across designers and programmers. narration.text: These three concise concepts are the backbone of the chapter. First, an abstract class contains pure virtual functions and enforces required implementations while allowing shared helpers. Second, a pure virtual function uses the equals-zero syntax to make the base class abstract and force derived classes to implement the method. Third, an interface describes what an object can do and is implemented with Unreal's UInterface pattern so any UCLASS can opt into the behavior. Remember these distinctions as you design systems: identity and shared code belong in abstract bases; orthogonal capabilities belong in interfaces. Use the Execute_ call at runtime to respect both C++ and Blueprint implementations and log clearly when objects do not implement expected behavior. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Abstract Class
Base type with pure virtuals; enforces derived implementations and can share helpers.
Pure Virtual Function
Declared with = 0; makes a class abstract and requires derived overrides.
UInterface
Unreal's interface pattern: UINTERFACE wrapper and I-prefixed C++ contract with UFUNCTIONs.
Takeaway
Design with identity, shared code, and orthogonal capability in mind. Use Execute_ and Implements checks to keep runtime calls safe and extensible.

narration.text: A short list of practical rules will help prevent errors. First, always use the I-prefixed interface name in C++ and include the generated header. Second, never call an interface function directly on an actor pointer expecting Blueprint overrides—always use the Execute_ dispatcher after checking Implements<UInterface>(). Third, prefer BlueprintNativeEvent for functions where you want a usable C++ default but still want designers to customize behavior in Blueprints. Avoid over-designing with many tiny interfaces; instead add interfaces where they provide clear decoupling and reuse. Finally, validate your interactions in-editor with log messages and on-screen debug messages so designers can iterate without a programmer changing code each time. These practices combine to make your game systems flexible and maintainable as projects scale. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
I-prefix
The C++ interface should begin with I, while the UINTERFACE has the U prefix.
Execute_ Dispatch
Use IInterface::Execute_Function to ensure the reflection system calls Blueprints or C++ implementations correctly.
BlueprintNativeEvent
Choose this specifier when you want to provide a C++ fallback and still allow Blueprint overrides.
Final takeaway
Combine abstract bases and interfaces thoughtfully: leverage shared code where appropriate and expose capabilities through interfaces to keep systems decoupled and easy to extend.
